correctness.rationale: For every existing affine resolvable 2-design AD(n,mu), n>=3, mu>=1, the actual incidence identities NN^T=s I+lambda J and N^T N=s I+mu(J-P) with s=n mu split the entire real zero-sum powered-distance form into (r-1) parallel scalars, (v-1) coupled 2x2 blocks and one point/block contrast, accounting for exactly v+b-1 dimensions. The parallel eigenvalue a((n-1)a-n) changes at p_par=log_2(n/(n-1)); the transversal block with diagonal -a,-a^2 has determinant a^3-s(3^p-1)^2 and one sharp positive threshold. The remaining contrast is <0 until p_par using convex endpoint estimates. The integer lambda forces mu=1 or mu>=n, and strict mean-value comparisons separate the two thresholds without accidental equality. Thus the claimed two-branch supremal p-negative type, strictness, endpoint nullities r-1 versus v-1, least Euclidean squared-distance dimensions and s^-1/2 asymptotic follow. The proof is for actual existing designs, not arbitrary admissible integers. Independent full-spectrum diagonalization and direct incidence reconstruction checked AG(2,3), AG(3,3), AG(2,5) on both sides of thresholds; these finite tests are diagnostics, not the all-design proof.

originality.rationale: Ma (2016) gives the ordinary unpowered p=1 distance characteristic polynomial of the same resolvable incidence graphs, and Sánchez gives general finite-metric negative-type methods. The research explicitly credits the already-known affine-plane branch, retaining as its substantive increment the higher-index mu>1 sharp powered-distance interval, strict two-obstruction phase separation, endpoint rank and embedding dimension. The prior p=1 spectrum does not logically determine the sign of the continuously powered distance matrix for all real p. No stronger prior covering the mu>1 sharp threshold was identified in the searched primary material, but a general powered-distance treatment of association schemes or design distance matrices is possible.
residual_risks: A historical general theorem for powered-distance kernels of affine resolvable association schemes may subsume the claimed higher-index result despite absent exact search matches.
Finite affine-geometry spectral checks cannot verify every existing non-Desarguesian design or the limit; those rely on the analytic identities.
